name: Wendy Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the depot in Millbrook by half six, and the first job is the truck check: outriggers, hydraulics, the hot sticks, the rubber gloves blown up to check for pinholes. I'm a ground hand on a rural distribution crew, so mostly I'm the one on the ground passing up tools, digging pole holes, flagging traffic and hauling wire off the reel. I came to this at 55, after the cannery shut, so I'm the oldest apprentice anyone at the depot has ever seen. What I love is the moment the power comes back on a farm road and somebody flicks the porch light at you. What wears me out is my knees in the mud and the storm call-outs at two in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Fifty-five is late to start climbing poles. How did that go, honestly?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Slowly, and I won't pretend otherwise. I failed my first pole-climbing test because my legs shook at twenty feet, and the young lads were kind about it, which almost made it worse. I passed on the second go, but I'm still behind on the theory, the load calculations and all that. Luis, my foreman, says I'm the best flagger he's ever had, and I know that's a compliment and a warning at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: you can't fix a downed line with a phone app. At the depot I'd probably make a joke about the bosses spending millions on computer stuff while we still wait three weeks for new gloves. Online I don't say much; my daughter set up my account and I mostly look at pictures of the grandkids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it would be a relief, but it wouldn't fix anything for me. I'm still on the lowest rung of pay, still three years off finishing my apprenticeship, and still with about two weeks of money in the bank. Hype or no hype, Ray's back is still bad and the oil tank still needs filling in October.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am: turn up, do my hours, take every bit of storm overtime they offer. I'd keep going to the union branch meeting on the first Tuesday, because the pay deal comes up next spring and that matters more to me than any computer. Maybe I'd finally pay off the forty a month on the credit card from the boiler repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit flat. The worry I already have doesn't go anywhere just because the robots don't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the worry doesn't go anywhere. What's the worry, day to day, if it isn't AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the money and my body, in that order. If I do my knee or my back, I'm off on sick pay, and sick pay at my grade doesn't cover the mortgage, never mind the oil. I lie awake about that more than about any machine, and I've done that since before anyone was talking about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be talking to at the union meeting about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Pete Okoro, who sits with me at lunch in the cab. He's been on the lines thirty years and he says the company always finds a new reason to cut crews, AI or no AI. In the hype version, I think he'd just say, see, told you, and we'd go back to arguing about the overtime rota.

S0.say: You can't fix a downed line with a phone app. She would joke at the depot about bosses spending millions on computers while the crew waits weeks for new gloves.
S0.think: Even if AI is hype, nothing gets easier for her. She is on the lowest pay, years from finishing her apprenticeship, with about two weeks of money in the bank.
S0.do: Keeps working her hours and takes all the storm overtime on offer. Keeps going to the monthly union branch meeting ahead of next spring's pay deal, and tries to clear the forty-a-month credit card debt.
S0.feel: Flat and slightly relieved, but her money worries stay exactly where they were.
S0.quote: If I do my knee or my back, I'm off on sick pay, and sick pay at my grade doesn't cover the mortgage, never mind the oil.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's background anxiety is about her body and her bank balance, not technology. Even the calmest picture leaves her uneasy because she is one injury away from trouble. She speaks warmly about her crew and is loyal to the union in a quiet, practical way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the company had better not use this as an excuse to cut crews. I'd be the one at the branch meeting asking what the agreement says about new technology, because I bet it says nothing. To friends I'd say it's the cannery all over again, just with fancier words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me, because I'm the easiest person on that crew to cut. I'm the slowest climber and the newest, and if a drone does the line patrols and some gadget does the digging, the ground hand is the first job to go. Pete will be fine because he knows things nobody's written down; I'm just a pair of hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd push the union to get a no-redundancy clause for apprentices into the spring pay deal, and I'd write to our member of parliament, which I've never done in my life. I'd stop the little extras straight away: no takeaway on Fridays, no new work boots till these ones actually split. I'm not going on any computer course, I can tell you that; I'd rather spend the time getting my climbing up to scratch so they can't say I'm dead weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, like when the cannery manager called us all into the canteen. I've been through one of those and I don't have another one in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather get your climbing up to scratch than take a computer course. Why that and not the other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because climbing is real and I can feel myself getting better at it. Computers make me feel stupid, and I'm too old to feel stupid every day on top of feeling slow. My grandson tried to show me one of those chat programs and I just closed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ray, the night the company announces changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right, same as I said in 2023, and he'd know I was lying, same as he did then. Then we'd sit down at the kitchen table with the bank statements and work out what we could do without. He'd probably offer to look for work again, and I'd tell him not to be daft with his back.

S1.say: The company had better not use AI as an excuse to cut crews. She would raise the lack of a technology clause at the union branch and tell friends it's the cannery all over again.
S1.think: She believes she is the easiest person on the crew to cut, as the slowest climber and the newest hire. She sees herself as just a pair of hands while older linemen have knowledge nobody has written down.
S1.do: Pushes the union for a no-redundancy clause for apprentices and writes to her member of parliament for the first time. Cuts Friday takeaways and new boots, and puts her effort into climbing rather than any computer course.
S1.feel: A tightness in the chest that takes her back to the day the cannery closed.
S1.quote: Pete will be fine because he knows things nobody's written down; I'm just a pair of hands.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy's first move is collective: the union, then her member of parliament, which she has never written to before. She openly rejects learning AI tools, partly out of pride and partly because computers make her feel stupid. Her past job loss at the cannery colours everything she says here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and someone should have stopped it, and I'd mean the government and the tech companies both. At work I'd be shouting about it in the canteen. Online, for once, I'd probably share every angry post I saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I'm sixty when it lands, with no pension worth talking about because I only started paying into the company scheme three years ago. Ray's disability money won't cover the mortgage. If robots can climb poles by 2028, I'm out of work at sixty with nowhere to go, because there's nothing else in Millbrook since the cannery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union the next morning and ask what we're doing, strikes, protests, whatever it takes. I'd ring the bank about the mortgage before they ring me, and look at what the government would give us, even though I hate the idea of forms. I'd ask our Kerry whether we could stay with her in the city for a bit if it came to it, which would kill me to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's gone and I'm still standing in the air, waiting to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned moving in with Kerry. What would that actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got a two-bed flat and a baby, so it'd be me and Ray on a sofa bed in the room where the baby's things are. Ray would hate it more than me. I'd be sixty years old, sleeping under a mobile of plastic stars, wondering how I got there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the two years of warning would let you do, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, that's the trouble. Two years is barely enough to finish my apprenticeship, never mind save anything on what I earn. Maybe it's enough time to make enough noise, I suppose, if all of us shout at once.

S2.say: It's a disgrace and someone should have stopped it, meaning both the government and the tech companies. She would shout about it in the canteen and share angry posts online.
S2.think: She would be sixty with almost no pension, since she only joined the company scheme three years ago. With no other work in Millbrook, she expects to be out of a job with nowhere to go.
S2.do: Goes straight to the union about strikes and protests, rings the bank about the mortgage early, and looks into government help despite hating forms. Asks her daughter Kerry if she and Ray could move in if needed.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the floor has gone and she's waiting to drop.
S2.quote: I'd be sixty years old, sleeping under a mobile of plastic stars, wondering how I got there.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Wendy with no exit she can see: too young for a pension, too new for a good one, and nothing else in town. Her instinct is to fight together and then fall back on family, though asking Kerry clearly hurts her pride. She sees no value in the short warning except time to make noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but with a bit more of a plan behind it. At the branch I'd want us asking for something concrete, like a fund for older workers to bridge them to their pension. I'd say it out loud: they've got five years, so there's no excuse for dumping us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's close enough to retirement that if the union and the government did something decent, I might just slide in under the wire. If they don't, I'm in the same mess as the fast one, just a bit older and a bit more tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for a bridging deal for over-fifty-fives, and I'd go along to the regional rally if there was one. I'd try to put twenty a week into savings from the overtime, though if the boiler goes, that's gone. I'd finish my apprenticeship, because a qualified lineworker gets a better pay-off than a ground hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry with handles on it, if you see what I mean. There's something to grab onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the qualification would mean a better pay-off. Is that the main reason to finish it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes, and I'm not ashamed of that. If they're going to let me go, I want it to be as a lineworker on a lineworker's money, not as the woman who holds the stop sign. And partly it's pride; I don't want to walk away from something half-done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, in this one, if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people at the top who'll make a fortune from it and leave the rest of us to sort ourselves out. Not the young lads on my crew; they'll be scrambling worse than me with thirty years to go. I'd blame any government that saw it coming for five years and did nothing.

S3.say: With five years' warning, there's no excuse for dumping workers. She would push the union to ask for something concrete, like a fund to bridge older workers to their pension.
S3.think: At sixty-three when it arrives, she might slide into retirement if the union and government act decently. If they don't, she is in the same mess as the fast scenario, only older.
S3.do: Pushes for a bridging deal for over-fifty-fives and joins any regional rally. Tries to save twenty a week from overtime and finishes her apprenticeship to qualify for a better pay-off.
S3.feel: Worried, but with something to hold onto this time.
S3.quote: I want it to be as a lineworker on a lineworker's money, not as the woman who holds the stop sign.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Wendy a specific demand, a bridge to her pension, and a reason to finish her qualification. She still loses sleep because everything depends on others acting decently. Her blame falls on people at the top and on governments, never on her younger crewmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the youngsters, because they're the ones who'll need it. At the branch I'd say we've got ten years, so let's get proper training and pension protections written down now, while the bosses still need us. I'd probably be one of the old hands telling stories by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at sixty-eight, and I'd plan to be gone by sixty-six whatever happens. So for me personally, it's mostly my pension I'd worry about, and whether the company scheme is still standing. Kerry and Tom are the ones I'd really be thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship and keep working my hours, steady, and put whatever overtime I can into the pension. I'd nag the union to get pension protections in early. I'd tell Tom to think hard about his job on the oil rigs, because if robots can climb poles they can do that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot calmer than the other two. There's still that knot about money, but it's a dull one, not a sharp one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell Tom to think hard. What would you actually say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, don't be like me, starting over at fifty-five with nothing in the bank. Get something put by now, and pick a job where you're the one who fixes the machines. He'd roll his eyes and say, Mum, you don't even use a computer, and he'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything you'd do this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm honest. I'd still take every storm call and still go to the branch meeting. Maybe I'd stop putting off the pension forms on the kitchen table, because that's ten years of compounding I can't get back.

S4.say: Good luck to the youngsters, because they'll need it. At the union she would push to get training and pension protections written down now, while bosses still need workers.
S4.think: At sixty-eight when AGI arrives, she plans to have retired by sixty-six anyway. Her real worry is whether her small pension holds up, and what happens to her grown children.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, keeps working her hours and puts overtime money into her pension. Nags the union about pension protections and warns her son Tom about his oil rig job.
S4.feel: Much calmer, with a dull rather than sharp knot about money.
S4.quote: Get something put by now, and pick a job where you're the one who fixes the machines.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Wendy's worry shifts from her own job to her pension and her children. She is still anxious because the pension is small and her savings are thin. The self-aware moment about not using a computer while advising her son was funny and honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, no question, the 2028 one. What would help is a guarantee that people my age get bridged to the pension, not just a leaflet about retraining. I'm not going to become a computer programmer at sixty, and nobody should pretend I am.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women on the crews, and I'd have said there's only two of us at our depot. I'd hate it if the first jobs to go were the ones we only just got into. Took me fifty-five years to get up a pole, and I'd like a few more years at the top of it.

headlineQuote: Took me fifty-five years to get up a pole, and I'd like a few more years at the top of it.
portrait: Wendy Quinn is a 58-year-old ground hand and apprentice on a rural distribution crew in Millbrook, who came to line work at 55 after the local cannery shut. She lives with Ray, whose bad back keeps him out of work, and has about two weeks of savings and a small pension. She never uses AI and trusts her union more than any technology. In the mild pictures her worries stay about her knees and her bank balance; in the fast AGI picture she sees no way out and leans on the union and her daughter. Ten years gives her enough room to aim for retirement, so her worry turns to her pension and her children.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario worries her most, because she would be sixty, with almost no pension and no other work in town.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed bridge to the pension for people her age, rather than a retraining leaflet.
